intent: The Mega Lucario line is the deck's only two-Prize-per-turn threat and Riolu is its bottleneck; Lunatone exists only to switch Solrock's attack on. Trade the second Lunatone for a fourth Riolu.
Boss's Orders is the deck's only way to reach the target the attack plan actually wants; the agent scores it 3200 and skips it when plan.target<1. Four Carmine is more draw than the curve needs.
Mega Brave needs two attachments and the agent attaches one per turn; a second Gravity Mountain is redundant once one has been played.
A public tuned build of this exact archetype (prvsiyan v12) differs from the official list by exactly these counts; test the whole published change as one arm.
Energy is the attack-readiness bottleneck and Poke Pad only draws; if the deck is losing to slow energy, more energy beats more looks at the deck.
The agent's plan can name a benched attacker but can only reach it through Switch or a retreat cost; a third Switch buys the plan more often than a second stadium.
Hariyama is the secondary 210-damage attacker; Solrock only attacks for 70 and only while Lunatone is in play.
Makuhita is the prerequisite for the Hariyama attacker the agent already prefers at three energy; the second Lunatone is the least-used card in the list.
Fighting Gong at four copies competes with basic energy for the same turn; trade one for the energy the attack actually needs.
Lillie's Determination and Carmine are both Supporters and only one Supporter is played per turn; the marginal fourth Lillie is often dead where Boss is not.
One Hero Cape is a singleton the agent finds only by drawing it; energy is never dead in a deck that attacks with two attachments.
Separate the two search effects: if Poke Pad's draw is what finds the line, a fourth Dusk Ball is the weaker copy.
Four Mega Lucario ex with three Riolu inverts the evolution line; the agent cannot play a Mega without its Riolu on board.
Combination arm: the two single changes most likely to be individually positive, to test whether they compose or compete.
